title: A critical view on transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans
funder: Work in the author's laboratory has been funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft.
authorConflicts: The author declares no competing interests.
result: Comment. Within a cell lineage, gene activity states are maintained over cell divisions; this cellular inheritance is attributed to regulatory feedback loops, chromatin modifications (DNA methylation and histone modifications) and long-lived non-coding RNAs. Chromatin is extensively reshaped during germ-cell differentiation and in totipotent cells after fertilisation. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans is a matter of controversial debate because genetic, ecological and cultural inheritance confound it; epidemiological links between grandparental food supply and grandchildren's health await independent replication; most families in which abnormal DNA methylation segregated with a rare disease proved to carry an underlying genetic variant; the excess cardiovascular and metabolic disease after prenatal exposure to the Dutch hunger winter is a direct consequence of exposure in utero, not germline transmission. The author concludes that the evidence is not (yet) conclusive.
